extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of mercantile arithmetic (merchants, bookkeepers)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional rules and procedures for manipulating fractions, finding common denominators, using proportionality, and applying these methods to merchant problems (currency conversion, exchange, partitioning). Historical/vernacular presentation aimed at practical computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplying fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiplying two fractions, multiply the numerators and the denominators (cross/multiplicative combination of parts); parts of the product represent corresponding parts of the original fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly explains multiplying 'Doi rotti' by taking numerators and denominators into account (e.g., 'chi multiplica Doi rotti in crocùcioe el Denominato de luno per lo Denominato de l'altro'). Examples show carrying through multiplicative parts and then taking particular parts of the resulting product to represent desired quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding fractions by common denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: To add fractions, bring them to the same denominator and then add the numerators; if the sum exceeds the denominator produce whole parts accordingly (the sum 'fara vn rotto' or a fraction representing the total).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: obtain a common denominator (via multiplication or suitable multiples), convert each fraction to that denominator (copying the 'riga' as needed), then sum numerators. The text illustrates forming a single fraction from multiple parts and reducing whole parts when numerators exceed the denominator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding a common denominator (product or multiples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common denominator may be obtained by multiplying the denominators together or by finding suitable multiples (least common multiples) so that all fractions can be expressed with the same denominator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the passage show using the product of denominators (producing values like '24o' in the worked examples) and also constructing multiples of denominators (listing successive multiples) until a shared denominator is found; then copying rows and aligning fractions to that denominator before summing or comparing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infilare / infilzare method (aligning partitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'infilare' (infilzare/infilzare) procedure: a technique of repeatedly inserting or aligning fractional parts (or numbers) into sequences so denominators or parts coincide for multiplication, partitioning, or comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains performing repeated 'infilzamenti' starting from a number or a fraction, continuing until parts 'coincidit cum'altri' (coincide with others). It notes one may need to find an intermediate number ('nome') so that the inserted parts match and computations proceed. Used when direct coincidence of parts is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partitioning and composing fractions via copies and multiplications
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing quantities into parts by position/order, form copies of rows and multiply appropriately so denominators represent the partitions; compose resulting parts into a single fraction or whole as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes making copies of a row corresponding to the desired denominator, multiplying rows by factors to produce comparable parts, and summing or partitioning those parts. This is the practical method for partitioning lots, shares, or composite quantities in mercantile arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using proportionality for currency conversion and exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply proportional rules to convert between currencies or values: multiply the given quantity by the rate (value of other currency) and divide by the unit; repeated multiplication/partitioning yields conversions between desired coinage or measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The long sections on Ducati, Denari, and other monies advise multiplying the 'rotto' by the currency's value, possibly by convenient scalars such as 100 or 240, then partitioning by the divisor representing the unit. Examples show converting via successive multiplications and partitions to obtain equivalent values in another currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solving proportions (rule of three and extended rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve proportions by forming products of corresponding terms (cross-products). For chains of proportions with more terms (three, four, etc.), use products of given terms and divide by the remaining knowns to find the unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains taking known terms, forming their product (or product of appropriate terms across the proportion), and dividing by the other known to recover the unknown. Examples include four-term problems where one forms products (e.g., of first and second known terms) and uses division to find the missing term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous vs. discontinuous proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish continuous (continua) proportional chains—where terms follow successively—and discontinuous (inconrinua) proportion; continuous proportion problems require considering sequences of terms and may need working through multiple intermediate terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author discusses finding relationships when proportions are 'continua' versus 'incontinua,' noting how continuous proportion may involve more than three terms and that solving requires handling products across the chain (e.g., first to fourth via intermediate multiplications). Guidance includes examples of how to arrange known and unknown terms in such chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling and choosing convenient multipliers to simplify computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale quantities by convenient multipliers (100, 240, etc.) to obtain integral or convenient denominators, making comparisons and partitions easier in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the merchant examples the text recommends multiplying by standard magnitudes (e.g., 100, 24, 240) to get manageable numbers for division and comparison. The method: choose multipliers that align with coinage or unit systems to reduce fractional complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical use of known units and tabular conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer using known unit-conversion tables and memorized rules (for coin, weight, measure) to transform problems into familiar units before performing proportional arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advises merchants to keep to memorized conversions ('le parti... a memoza') and to consult regular figures/tables; employing such standard conversions reduces arithmetic effort and errors in trade calculations. Examples show forming tables of multiples and using them to find products or partitions.
